 Frequently Asked Questions

 Q1. How much ground clearance is legally or practically enough for Indian cities?

Any car with 170 mm to 180 mm of unladen ground clearance and well-damped suspension will handle 98% of city and national highway speed breakers without scraping. You only need 200+ mm if you regularly drive with 5 adults + full boot luggage over broken village roads or unpaved construction zones.

 Q2. Why did the Honda Elevate get 220 mm ground clearance when the Honda City has 165 mm?

Although both share Honda's Global Small Car platform, Honda re-engineered the Elevate with longer-travel struts, reshaped lower control arms, and taller 215/55 R17 tyres specifically to give Indian SUV buyers class-leading 220 mm clearance.

 Q3. Can I increase my car's ground clearance using rubber coil-spring buffers ('Rogerab')?

Aftermarket urethane spring buffers reduce suspension compression under load by stiffening the middle coils, but they restrict natural suspension travel and place uneven stress on the spring coils. It is safer to maintain correct factory full-load tyre pressures (+2–3 PSI for full load as printed on your door jamb).

 Q4. Do Electric Vehicles (EVs) have lower ground clearance because of the battery pack?

Yes, typically by 10 to 18 mm compared to their petrol siblings. For example, while the petrol Tata Nexon has 208 mm ground clearance, the Nexon EV sits at 190–205 mm depending on the battery pack because the high-voltage battery enclosure is mounted beneath the floor.

 Q5. Does installing slightly taller profile tyres safely increase ground clearance?

Upsizing tyre sidewall height within the safe 2% overall diameter limit (for example, moving from 205/55 R16 to 205/60 R16 after your factory tyres wear out) can add roughly 8 to 10 mm of true axle ground clearance and soften the ride slightly without affecting speedometer calibration or wheel-well clearance.

1. Less Motion Sickness on Highways & Hills: Because an SUV sits 150–200 mm taller, its higher centre of gravity creates greater lateral head-toss when cornering or changing lanes. 1. Massive Sealed Luggage Boots: A Hyundai Verna (528L), Skoda Slavia/VW Virtus (521L), or Honda City (506L) holds 80 to 145 litres more luggage than its SUV twin—and keeps dusty suitcases sealed away from the air-conditioned passenger cabin.
1. Aerodynamic Highway Efficiency & ₹2 Lakh Price Savings: Pushing a sleek sedan through the air at 100 km/h requires 12% less power than pushing a tall, boxy SUV grille, yielding 1.5–2.5 km/l higher highway mileage.

 Frequently Asked Questions

 Q1. Why do the Volkswagen Virtus and Skoda Slavia rarely scrape on Indian roads?

Both the Virtus and Slavia were engineered specifically on the India-2.0 MQB-A0-IN platform with 179 mm of unladen ground clearance and firm German spring/damper rates—giving them practically the same underbody clearance as many soft-roader crossovers.

 Q2. Which body style has better crash-test safety in India: SUV or Sedan?

Both body styles now achieve top 5-star scores. The Hyundai Verna, Volkswagen Virtus, Skoda Slavia, and new Maruti Dzire all hold 5-star Global NCAP ratings, matching 5-star SUVs like the Nexon, XUV 3XO, Kushaq, Taigun, and XUV700.

 Q3. Do SUVs hold higher resale value in India than sedans?

Currently, mass-market SUVs (like the Creta and Brezza) retain roughly 4% to 7% higher percentage resale value after 5 years than mid-size sedans. However, because you pay ₹1.50–₹2.50 lakh less upfront for a sedan (plus lower road tax and insurance), your total rupee depreciation is very similar.

 Q4. Why do rear passengers feel more comfortable in a Honda City or Hyundai Verna than in a mid-size SUV?

Sedans have a longer rear seat cushion with a more reclined backrest angle (around 27 degrees) and lower floor-to-hip geometry that supports your thighs naturally like a living-room sofa, whereas SUV seats position you more upright like a dining chair.

 Q5. What is the safe water-wading depth difference between a sedan and an SUV?

A typical sedan can safely wade through 250–300 mm of standing water (up to the bottom of the door sills or wheel hubs), whereas most monocoque SUVs can handle 350–400 mm (and dedicated off-roaders like the Thar Roxx or Gurkha handle 650–700 mm).

 Q2. What happens to luggage space in a Maruti Ertiga S-CNG?

 Frequently Asked Questions

 Q1. Why are the Skoda Kushaq and Volkswagen Taigun not ideal for 5 adults?

The Kushaq and Taigun are exceptional 4-adult drivers' cars with 5-star Global NCAP ratings, but their narrower 1,760 mm width and deeply contoured outer rear seats leave a narrow, raised perch in the middle that is only comfortable for a child.

 Q2. Why does the Maruti Grand Vitara Strong Hybrid have a smaller boot than the normal petrol version?

In the Strong Hybrid variants of the Grand Vitara and Toyota Hyryder, the lithium-ion hybrid battery pack sits underneath the boot floor, reducing luggage capacity from 373 litres down to roughly 265 litres—which is tight for five people's weekend suitcases.

 Q3. Is it safe to place a child car seat in the middle rear seat?

ISOFIX anchor rings in Indian cars are mounted on the two outer rear seats (behind the driver and front passenger). When you install an ISOFIX child seat on one outer seat, its wide side wings occupy about 40% of the bench, leaving comfortable room for two slim adults beside it in wider cars like the Creta or XUV700.

 Q4. Does the Mahindra XUV700 fit under ₹20 lakh on-road?

Yes. The 5-seater and 7-seater MX and AX3/AX5 petrol manual variants—as well as MX diesel trims—fit within ₹16.20 lakh to ₹20.10 lakh on-road depending on your state's road tax.

 Q5. Which car under ₹20 lakh has the strongest air conditioning for all 5 passengers?

The Kia Carens (with roof-mounted diffused AC vents for the second and third rows) and the Hyundai Creta / Kia Seltos cools rear cabins fastest during peak 44°C North Indian summers.

 Frequently Asked Questions

 Q1. Is a sedan like the VW Virtus or Honda City less tiring on highways than a tall SUV?

On well-paved 4-to-6-lane expressways, a sedan with a lower centre of gravity pitches and rolls significantly less during lane changes and curves than a tall SUV, reducing inner-ear motion fatigue for passengers.

 Q2. Does Level-2 ADAS actually work on Indian expressways?

Yes. On access-controlled highways with painted lane markings (like the Mumbai-Pune, Samruddhi, or Delhi-Mumbai expressways), Adaptive Cruise Control with Stop & Go and Lane Centering Assist in the XUV700, Creta, and Harrier noticeably reduce right-foot and steering fatigue—though the driver must keep hands on the wheel at all times.

 Q3. Why is Diesel still preferred over Turbo-Petrol for heavy SUV highway touring?

A 1.7-to-2.0-tonne turbo-petrol SUV (like the XUV700 Petrol AT or Scorpio-N Petrol AT) typically returns 10–12 km/l on highways, requiring fuel stops every 480–550 km. Their diesel counterparts return 15–17 km/l, stretching range past 800 km with stronger low-RPM climbing torque.

 Q4. What if I live in Delhi NCR and want a highway car with a 15-year lifespan?

If you want to avoid the 10-year NCR diesel restriction while still getting 800+ km highway range, pick either the VW Virtus / Skoda Slavia 1.5 TSI (which achieves 17–19 km/l on petrol via cylinder deactivation) or the Toyota Innova Hycross / Maruti Grand Vitara Strong Hybrid.

 Q5. Which highway car has the best service support across remote parts of India?

Maruti Suzuki (Grand Vitara), Hyundai (Creta), and Mahindra (XUV700, Scorpio-N) have the densest highway and district-level workshop networks across India if you ever face a tyre, battery, or mechanical issue on a cross-country road trip.

In India, a new car's true mandatory on-road price equals the Ex-Showroom Price (which already includes factory cost, GST, and dealer margin) plus State RTO Road Tax and Registration Fees, Compulsory Motor Insurance (3-year third-party + 1-year own-damage), a ₹500–₹600 FASTag, Hypothecation Fee (₹1,500 if financed), and 1% Tax Collected at Source (TCS) if the ex-showroom price exceeds ₹10,00,000. Accessories, ceramic coatings, and logistics/handling fees are not legally mandatory.


 The 5 Mandatory Building Blocks of an Indian On-Road Price


When a salesperson hands you a price quotation (proforma invoice), separate the numbers into statutory requirements versus dealership profit centres:

1. Ex-Showroom Price: Set by the automaker for your city. It already includes the ex-factory price, Goods and Services Tax (GST plus Compensation Cess ranging from 29% on small petrol cars to 50% on large SUVs), freight to the dealership, and the dealer's base margin.
1. State RTO Road Tax & Registration: Collected by the state transport department. It varies dramatically by state—ranging from roughly 4%–8% on petrol cars in Delhi/Himachal to 11%–14% in Maharashtra and 14%–20% in Karnataka and Telangana. Also includes a ₹600 smart-card RC fee, ₹400–₹600 High Security Registration Plate (HSRP) charge, and ₹1,500 hypothecation endorsement if you take a car loan.
1. 1% TCS (Tax Collected at Source): Under Section 206C(1F) of the Income Tax Act, if a car's ex-showroom invoice exceeds ₹10,00,000 (even at ₹10,01,000), the dealer must collect 1% TCS (₹10,010+). Crucial fact: This is NOT an extra tax; it appears in your Form 26AS and can be claimed back or adjusted against your annual income tax liability when filing your ITR.
1. Motor Insurance (1-Year OD + 3-Year TP): By Supreme Court mandate, every new private car must carry 3 years of Third-Party (TP) liability cover, typically bundled with 1 year of Own-Damage (OD) plus Zero-Depreciation, Return-to-Invoice (RTI), and Engine Protector add-ons.
1. FASTag: Mandatory toll tag costing ₹400–₹600 (including security deposit and initial balance).

 Frequently Asked Questions

No. Under IRDAI and Competition Commission principles, a dealer cannot force you to buy insurance through their in-house broker.  Q2. Why did my car's on-road price jump by ₹45,000 when the ex-showroom price increased by only ₹10,000 across ₹10 lakh?

Cross-stepping the ₹10,00,000 ex-showroom mark triggers two simultaneous jumps in most Indian states: the state road tax slab typically increases by 2%–3% on the entire vehicle value, and the 1% TCS (₹10,000+) becomes payable upfront.

 Q3. What is BH-Series registration and how does it reduce upfront on-road price?

If you are a central/state government employee or work for a private company with offices in four or more states/UTs, Bharat (BH) Series registration lets you pay road tax in 2-year instalments instead of a 15-year lump sum, reducing your day-one on-road cash outlay by ₹60,000 to ₹1.50 lakh.

 Q4. Is Extended Warranty worth keeping on the invoice?

Yes. Unlike paint coatings or chrome kits, an official manufacturer Extended Warranty (covering years 4 and 5) protects expensive AC compressors, steering racks, and infotainment modules and is fully transferable if you sell the car.

 Q5. Should I get the Parivahan tax receipt from the dealer?

Always collect the official Parivahan e-receipt for road tax and registration at delivery. Verify that the exact tax paid to the government matches what the dealership billed you on the proforma invoice.

 AMT vs CVT Under ₹10 Lakh: Why Gearbox Type Changes Your Daily Drive


Not all 'two-pedal' cars under ₹10 lakh work the same way beneath the floor. Knowing which gearbox is fitted prevents buyer's remorse:

- AMT (Automated Manual Transmission — called AGS by Maruti, Smart Auto by Hyundai): Uses a standard manual gearbox and clutch operated by electro-hydraulic or electric actuators. AMTs cost only ₹50,000–₹65,000 more than a manual and deliver nearly identical fuel efficiency. However, you will feel a brief pause ('head-nod') during 1st-to-2nd and 2nd-to-3rd upshifts under hard throttle.
- CVT / IVT (Continuously Variable / Intelligent Variable Transmission): Uses two variable-diameter pulleys connected by a steel belt or chain instead of fixed gear cogs. There are zero gear changes and zero shift shocks in bumper-to-bumper traffic. A CVT costs ₹90,000–₹1,20,000 more than a manual and typically consumes 1–2 km/l more petrol in dense city crawls.

 Frequently Asked Questions

 Q1. How can I reduce the gear-shift jerk ('head-nod') when driving an AMT car?

Ease off the accelerator pedal slightly for half a second just as the car reaches 2,000–2,200 RPM between 1st and 2nd gear, exactly as you would in a manual car. This lets the actuator complete the shift smoothly without lurching.

 Q2. Is an AMT clutch expensive to replace compared to a manual clutch?

The mechanical clutch plate and pressure plate inside an AMT wear out just like a manual clutch (typically lasting 45,000–70,000 km) and cost roughly ₹6,000–₹10,000 to replace. However, avoid holding the car stationary on slopes using the accelerator, which overheats the clutch.

 Q3. Should I shift an automatic into Neutral (N) at long Indian traffic signals?

Yes. If you are stopped at a red light for more than 20–30 seconds, shifting to Neutral (N) and engaging the handbrake releases actuator/transmission load and reduces brake pedal fatigue.

 Q4. Why are there no Torque Converter or DCT automatics under ₹10 lakh on-road?

Torque converter (AT) and dual-clutch (DCT) gearboxes are paired with higher-taxed turbo-petrol engines in cars like the Venue DCT, Sonet DCT, Brezza AT, and XUV 3XO AT, whose automatic trims start between ₹11.50 lakh and ₹13.20 lakh on-road.

 Q5. Does a CVT rubber-band effect matter in city driving?

No. The CVT 'rubber-band' sensation—where engine RPM rises before road speed catches up—only occurs when you floor the accelerator for sudden highway overtakes. In gentle city driving, a CVT is exceptionally smooth and quiet.

 Frequently Asked Questions

 Q1. Which car in India has the smallest turning radius?

Among four-wheeled passenger cars currently on sale, the MG Comet EV has the tightest turning radius at 4.2 metres, followed by the Maruti Suzuki Alto K10 and S-Presso at 4.5 metres.

 Q2. Why is vehicle width so important for parking in Indian apartment basements?

Older apartment complexes in Indian metro cities often have pillar-to-pillar parking bays designed 15–20 years ago for narrower cars. A car under 1,690 mm wide gives you an extra 100–120 mm of door-opening clearance compared to a 1,800 mm compact SUV.

 Q3. Is the Maruti Ignis better than the Swift for narrow city lanes?

Yes. The Ignis is 160 mm shorter and 45 mm narrower than the Swift, sits 17 mm higher off the ground (180 mm vs 163 mm) for clearing rough speed breakers, and uses a smooth four-cylinder 1.2-litre engine.

 Q4. Are AMT automatics good enough for bumper-to-bumper city traffic?

Modern AMTs in the Grand i10 Nios, Ignis, Celerio, and Tiago have calibrated creep functions that let you inch forward in traffic simply by releasing the brake pedal, saving your left knee from hundreds of daily clutch presses.

 Q5. Should I add a 360-degree or rear camera to a small city car?

A clear factory rear parking camera with dynamic guidelines plus rear ultrasonic sensors is more than sufficient for sub-3.8-metre cars and makes tight parallel parking effortless.
